name: nvFuser (MosaicML fusion compiler, now under NVIDIA)
license: NOASSERTION - NVIDIA's BSD-style LICENSE with bundled third-party attributions (PyTorch, Caffe2 and others); no standard SPDX id
production_evidence: PyTorch shipped nvFuser as a torch.compile backend for years - the PyTorch foundation itself announced it as a PyTorch deep learning compiler
Published on PyPI and NVIDIA's own index (pypi.nvidia.com), with stable wheels built against PyTorch stable releases
strengths: Whole-subgraph fusion rather than elementwise-only fusion, which is what made it worth building before Triton existed
Handles dynamic inputs of varying shapes and strides, which is the actual difficulty in serving
Targets Volta and later, i.e. a wider floor than tools that need Hopper-era features
weaknesses: The binding to PyTorch is the whole problem: wheels are built against a specific PyTorch stable or nightly, so compiler and framework versions must move together
The [torch] extra 'will REPLACE your existing PyTorch installation with a compatible nightly build' - an install step that can silently downgrade a production environment
Does not support all PyTorch operations; NVIDIA's own announcement carries that caveat
Version-pinned to CUDA 12.6+ wheels, a different floor from Triton at CC 8.0+, so the two NVIDIA kernel toolchains are not interchangeable
Last push 2026-05-31 with no GitHub release object and a 406-star public mirror - the public repo is not where most of the work happens, so community support is thin
notes: Provenance matters here and is the reason this record exists separately from the existing torch-compile-torchinductor record: nvFuser is MosaicML's fusion compiler, announced by the PyTorch foundation in 2022 and later donated to NVIDIA, which now hosts NVIDIA/Fuser. It is a graph optimizer in the schema's sense - it fuses groups of eager PyTorch operations into generated CUDA kernels rather than exposing a language to write kernels in. The documented flow is analyze the ops running on GPU, plan parallelization, apply the strategies in generated code, runtime-compile the generated functions, then execute those CUDA kernels on subsequent iterations. autotuning is false: nvFuser applies its own planned strategies, it does not search a configuration space per kernel the way @triton.autotune does. Its optimisation is whole-subgraph, which is a different axis from per-kernel tuning, and conflating the two is the usual source of confused claims. For a planner the practical point is the coupling, not the codegen: the wheel-to-PyTorch-version binding and the [torch] extra's PyTorch replacement behaviour mean nvFuser is a build-time choice that has to be pinned deliberately, and a nightly-index install can change the PyTorch underneath an unrelated service. compile_time_seconds is null because no primary source gives a per-kernel figure for it.
